text: THIS BOOK is an attempt at a consistent philosophy of life.
text_raw: THIS BOOK is an attempt at a consistent philosophy of life.

text: It tries to do for the problems of philosophy what The Story of Philosophy sought to do for the personalities and systems of the major philosophers—to make them intelligible by transparent speech, and to vitalize them by con- temporary application.

for the problems of philosophy what The Story of Philosophy sought to
do for the personalities and systems of the major philosophers—to make
them intelligible by transparent speech, and to vitalize them by con-
temporary application.

text: It is the age of Socrates again: our moral life is threatened, and our intellectual life is quickened and enlarged, by the disintegration of ancient customs and beliefs.

age of Socrates again: our moral life is threatened, and our intellectual life

text: Everything is new and experimental in our ideas and our actions; nothing is established or certain any more.

text: The rate, complexity, and vari- ety of change in our time are without precedent, even in Periclean days; all forms about us are altered, from the tools that complicate our toil, and the wheels that whirl us restlessly about the earth, to the innovations in our sexual relationships, and the hard disillusionment of our souls.

text: In every developing civilization a period comes when old instincts and habits prove inadequate to altered stimuli, and ancient institutions and moralities crack like hampering shells under the obstinate growth of life.

text: In one sphere after another, now that we have left the farm and the home for the factory, the office and the world, spontaneous and “natural” modes of order and response break down, and intellect chaotically experi- ments to replace with conscious guidance the ancestral readiness and sim- plicity of impulse and wonted ways.

ments to replace with conscious guidance the ancestral readiness and sim-
plicity of impulse and wonted ways.

text: The happy unity of instinct is gone from us, and we flounder in a sea of reasoning and doubt; in the midst of unprecedented knowledge and power we are uncertain of our purposes, our values, and our goals.

text: Then we shall leap into the metaphysical center of things, and make up our minds about ma- terialism; we shall see, if we may, whether thought is a function of matter, and whether choice is the delusion of a transiently animated machine.

text: From that focus we shall adventure into the realm of ethics, and inquire into the nature of the good life; we shall seek the causes and forecast the re- sults of our changing morals, our dissolving marriage, and our loosened love; we shall discuss the modern woman without gallantry, and without revenge; we shall confront Zeno with Epicurus, and search for the haunts of happiness; and we shall bring our findings together for the guidance of education and the reconstruction of character.

text: Then political philosophy will lure us, and we shall find ourselves de- bating, as in our passionate youth, the problems of anarchism, communism, socialism, conservatism, democracy, aristocracy, and dictatorship.

text: Why have her children, the sciences, divided her inheritance, and turned her out of doors, like another Lear, with ingratitude unkinder than the winter’s wind?
text_raw:
Why have her children, the
sciences, divided her inheritance, and turned her out of doors, like another
Lear, with ingratitude unkinder than the winter’s wind?

text: Once the strongest men were willing to die for her:
text_raw: Once the strongest men were willing to die for her:

text: Socrates chose to be her martyr rather than live in flight before her enemies;
text_raw:
Socrates chose to
be her martyr rather than live in flight before her enemies;

text: Plato risked himself twice to win a kingdom for her;
text_raw:
Plato risked
himself twice to win a kingdom for her;

text: Marcus Aurelius loved her more passionately than his throne; and Bruno burned at the stake for loyalty to her.
text_raw:
Marcus Aurelius loved her more
passionately than his throne; and Bruno burned at the stake for loyalty to
her.

text: Once thrones and papacies feared philosophy and imprisoned her vo- taries lest dynasties should fall.
text_raw:
Once thrones and papacies feared philosophy and imprisoned her vo-
taries lest dynasties should fall.

text: Athens exiled Protagoras, and Alexandria trembled before Hypatia; a great pope courted timidly the friendship of Erasmus; regents and kings hounded Voltaire from their lands, and fretted in jealousy when at last all the civilized world bowed before the sceptre of his pen.
text_raw:
Athens exiled Protagoras, and Alexandria
trembled before Hypatia; a great pope courted timidly the friendship of
Erasmus; regents and kings hounded Voltaire from their lands, and fretted
in jealousy when at last all the civilized world bowed before the sceptre of
his pen.

text: Dionysius and Dionysius’ son offered Plato the mastery of Syra- cuse;
text_raw:
Dionysius and Dionysius’ son offered Plato the mastery of Syra-
cuse;

text: Alexander’s royal aid made Aristotle the most learned man in history, a scholar-king lifted Francis Bacon almost to the leadership of England, and protected him from his enemies; and the great Frederick, at midnight when all his pompous generals had gone to sleep, held high revelry with poets and philosophers, envious of their boundless realms and their timeless sway.
text_raw:
Alexander’s royal aid made Aristotle the most learned man in history,
a scholar-king lifted Francis Bacon almost to the leadership of England,
and protected him from his enemies; and the great Frederick, at midnight
when all his pompous generals had gone to sleep, held high revelry with
poets and philosophers, envious of their boundless realms and their timeless
sway.

text: Those were great days for philosophy when bravely she took all knowl- edge for her province, and threw herself at every turn into the forefront of the mind’s advance.
text_raw:
Those were great days for philosophy when bravely she took all knowl-
edge for her province, and threw herself at every turn into the forefront of
the mind’s advance.

text: Men honored her then; nothing was held nobler than the love of truth.
text_raw:
Men honored her then; nothing was held nobler than
the love of truth.

text_raw: 2 | The Pleasures of Philosophy

text: Diogenes bade Alexander stand aside lest his royal carcass should hide the sun.

Diogenes bade Alexander stand aside lest his royal carcass should hide the

text: Statesmen and thinkers and artists listened gladly to Aspasia, and ten thousand students made long pilgrimages to Paris to learn from Abélard.

text: Philosophy was not then a timid spinster hiding in locked towers from the rough usage of the world; her bright eyes did not fear the day; she lived dangerously, and made distant voyages into unknown seas.
text_raw:
Philosophy was not then a timid spinster hiding in locked towers from the
rough usage of the world; her bright eyes did not fear the day; she lived
dangerously, and made distant voyages into unknown seas.

text: Could she ever, in those years when she held court before monarchs, have contented herself with the narrow boundaries within which to-day she has been imprisoned?
text_raw:
Could she ever,
in those years when she held court before monarchs, have contented herself
with the narrow boundaries within which to-day she has been imprisoned?

text: Once she was a many-colored light that filled with warmth and radiance the profoundest souls; now she is the ignominious satellite of fragmentary sci- ences and scholastic disciplines.
text_raw:
Once she was a many-colored light that filled with warmth and radiance the
profoundest souls; now she is the ignominious satellite of fragmentary sci-
ences and scholastic disciplines.

text: Once she was proud mistress of all the in- tellectual globe, and counted the loftiest among her happy servitors; now, despoiled of her beauty and her power, she stands by the wayside desolate, and none so poor to do her reverence.*
text_raw:
Once she was proud mistress of all the in-
tellectual globe, and counted the loftiest among her happy servitors; now,
despoiled of her beauty and her power, she stands by the wayside desolate,
and none so poor to do her reverence.*

text: Philosophy is not loved to-day because she has lost the spirit of adventure.
text_raw: Philosophy is not loved to-day because she has lost the spirit of adventure.

text: The sudden uprising of the sciences has stolen from her, one by one, her ancient spacious realms. “Cosmology” has become astronomy and geology; “natural philosophy” has become biology and physics; and in our own day the “philosophy of mind” has budded into psychology.
text_raw:
The sudden uprising of the sciences has stolen from her, one by one, her
ancient spacious realms. “Cosmology” has become astronomy and geology;
“natural philosophy” has become biology and physics; and in our own day
the “philosophy of mind” has budded into psychology.

text: All the real and cru- cial problems have escaped from her: no longer does she concern herself with the nature of matter and the secret of vitality and growth; the “‘will” whose “freedom” she debated in a hundred wars of thought has been crushed in the mechanism of modern life; the state, whose problems were once her own, is the happy hunting ground of petty souls, and less than ever honors the counsels of philosophy.
text_raw:
All the real and cru-
cial problems have escaped from her: no longer does she concern herself with
the nature of matter and the secret of vitality and growth; the “‘will” whose
“freedom” she debated in a hundred wars of thought has been crushed in
the mechanism of modern life; the state, whose problems were once her own,
is the happy hunting ground of petty souls, and less than ever honors the
counsels of philosophy.

text: Nothing remains to her except the cold peaks of metaphysics, the childish puzzles of epistemology, and the academic disputes of an ethics that has lost all influence on mankind.
text_raw:
Nothing remains to her except the cold peaks of
metaphysics, the childish puzzles of epistemology, and the academic disputes
of an ethics that has lost all influence on mankind.

text: Even these wastes will be taken from her; new sciences will rise and enter these territories with compass and microscope and rule; and perhaps the world will forget that philosophy ever existed, or ever moved the hearts and guided the minds of men.
text_raw:

be taken from her; new sciences will rise and enter these territories with
compass and microscope and rule; and perhaps the world will forget that

text: The simple conceptions of nineteenth-century physics and chemistry made the gap between living and non-living things im- passable; and even Spencer, though eager to make evolution complete, was compelled to shirk the problem, and to write: ‘We are obliged to confess that Life in its essence cannot be conceived in physico-chemical terms.” + When physics and chemistry learn to accept the concept of life as coterminous with the concept of matter, the division of reality and development into irreconcilable halves disappears; and a matter whose core is vitality com- bines with a life whose form is matter, to give to the world that complete unity and complete harmony without which neither science nor philosophy will ever rest.

text: Let us take note, in closing, that the naive mechanical approach is break- ing down in philosophy, in biology, in psychology, in physiology, even in physics itself. “Today,” says Lucien Poincaré, “the idea that all phenomena are capable of mechanical explanations is generally abandoned.” 1 “In modern physics,” says Cassirer, “the mechanical view of the world has been more and more superseded and replaced by the electro-dynamic view.” ? “In spite of the efforts of thousands of workers,” says Le Bon, “physiology has been able to tell us nothing of the nature of the forces” that produce the phenomena of life. “They have no analogy with those that are studied in physics.” * As chemistry needs the concept of quality in addition to that concept of quantity with which physics tries to be content, so physiology needs, in addition to quantity and quality, the concepts of organism and totality.

text: A remarkable sentence in The Advancement of Learning contains in outline an entire theory of secular ethics. “All things,” says the great Chancellor, “are endued with an appetite to two kinds of good—the one as this thing is a whole in itself” (this appetite we call the individualistic instincts), “the other as it is part of some greater whole” (this other appetite we call the social instincts); “and this latter is more worthy and more powerful than the other, as it tends to the conservation of a more ample form.’ That is to say, morality, like immorality, has its basis in human nature; there are social as well as egoistic impulses, instincts for group and race preserva- tion, as well as for self-preservation ; and these social instincts, Bacon thinks, are ultimately stronger than the instincts that aim to preserve the individual.

generations, and elude the enmity of death.

text: Thirty generations passed, and Leonardo da Vinci, spirit made flesh, scratched across his draw- ings (drawings so beautiful that one catches one’s breath with pain in seeing them) plans and calculations for a flying machine; and left in his notes a little phrase that, once heard, rings like a bell in the memory— “There shall be wings.’ Leonardo failed and died; but life carried on the dream.

text: A Note About the Author
text_raw: A Note About the Author

text: Witt Durant was born in North Adams, Massachusetts, in 1885, of French- Canadian parents.
text_raw:
Witt Durant was born in North Adams, Massachusetts, in 1885, of French-
Canadian parents.

text: He was educated in Catholic parochial schools there and in New Jersey, at St. Peter’s (Jesuit) College in Jersey City, and at Colum- bia University, New York.
text_raw:
He was educated in Catholic parochial schools there and
in New Jersey, at St. Peter’s (Jesuit) College in Jersey City, and at Colum-
bia University, New York.

text: For a summer he served as cub reporter on the New York Journal ; but finding himself unfit for this exciting work, he sub- sided into teaching Latin, French, English, and geometry at Seton Hall College, South Orange, New Jersey (1907-11).
text_raw:
For a summer he served as cub reporter on the
New York Journal ; but finding himself unfit for this exciting work, he sub-
sided into teaching Latin, French, English, and geometry at Seton Hall
College, South Orange, New Jersey (1907-11).

text: He entered the seminary there in 1909, but withdrew in 1911 for reasons which he has described in his book Transition.
text_raw:
He entered the seminary
there in 1909, but withdrew in 1911 for reasons which he has described in
his book Transition.

text: From this seminary he passed at one leap to the most radical circles in New York and became the “principal, teacher, and chief pupil” of the Ferrer Modern School (1911-13), an experiment in libertarian education.
text_raw:
From this seminary he passed at one leap to the most
radical circles in New York and became the “principal, teacher, and chief
pupil” of the Ferrer Modern School (1911-13), an experiment in libertarian
education.

text: In 1912 he toured Europe from Killarney to Yalta at the ex- pense of Alden Freeman, who had befriended him and had undertaken to broaden his borders.
text_raw:
In 1912 he toured Europe from Killarney to Yalta at the ex-
pense of Alden Freeman, who had befriended him and had undertaken to
broaden his borders.

text: In 1913 he gave himself over to graduate studies at Columbia University, specializing in biology under Morgan and Calkins, and in philosophy under Woodbridge and Dewey.
text_raw:
In 1913 he gave himself over to graduate studies at
Columbia University, specializing in biology under Morgan and Calkins,
and in philosophy under Woodbridge and Dewey.

text: In 1914, in a Presbyterian church at Fourteenth Street and Second Avenue, New York, he began those lectures on philosophy, literature, his- tory, science, and art which prepared him for The Story of Philosophy; the lectures published under this title astonished their author and publishers by becoming a best seller for years.
text_raw:
In 1914, in a Presbyterian church at Fourteenth Street and Second
Avenue, New York, he began those lectures on philosophy, literature, his-
tory, science, and art which prepared him for The Story of Philosophy; the
lectures published under this title astonished their author and publishers
by becoming a best seller for years.

text: In 1921 he organized the Labor Temple School and soon made it a thriving center of adult education.
text_raw:
In 1921 he organized the Labor Temple
School and soon made it a thriving center of adult education.

text: Relieved from scholastic work by the success of The Story of Philosophy, he retired in 1927 to devote his life to writing a history of civilization.
text_raw:
Relieved
from scholastic work by the success of The Story of Philosophy, he retired
in 1927 to devote his life to writing a history of civilization.

text: He toured Europe again in 1927; went around the world in 1930 to study Egypt, the Near East, India, China, and Japan; and circled the globe again in 1932 to 445

text: After seven years of travel and research he published in 1935 Our Oriental Heritage, the first volume of The Story of Civilization.
text_raw:
After seven years of
travel and research he published in 1935 Our Oriental Heritage, the first
volume of The Story of Civilization.

text: Having visited Greece and Italy in 1912, 1927, and 1930, he returned to them in 1936 and added firsthand studies to the rigorous training that he had received from the Jesuits in the classic languages and literatures.
text_raw:
Having visited Greece and Italy in
1912, 1927, and 1930, he returned to them in 1936 and added firsthand
studies to the rigorous training that he had received from the Jesuits in
the classic languages and literatures.

text: In 1939 he published The Life of Greece, and in 1944 Caesar and Christ.
text_raw:
In 1939 he published The Life of
Greece, and in 1944 Caesar and Christ.

text: In 1948 he spent six months in Europe and the Near and Middle East, studying medieval Christian and Moslem sites and remains from Edinburgh to Shiraz; and in 1950 he pub- lished The Age of Faith, a history of medieval civilization—Christian, Islamic, and Judaic—from Constantine to Dante.
text_raw:
In 1948 he spent six months in
Europe and the Near and Middle East, studying medieval Christian and
Moslem sites and remains from Edinburgh to Shiraz; and in 1950 he pub-
lished The Age of Faith, a history of medieval civilization—Christian,
Islamic, and Judaic—from Constantine to Dante.

text: In 1951 he spent seven months in Italy and France and studied nearly all the scenes and art de- scribed in Te Renaissance, the fifth volume of The Story of Civilization, published in the fall of 1953.
text_raw:
In 1951 he spent seven
months in Italy and France and studied nearly all the scenes and art de-
scribed in Te Renaissance, the fifth volume of The Story of Civilization,
published in the fall of 1953.

text: Dr. Durant is currently at work on the seventh and concluding volume of The Story of Civilization; entitled The Age of Reason, this will bring the story down to Napoleon and 1800, and the author plans to have it ready for publication around 1962.
text_raw:
Dr. Durant is currently at work on the
seventh and concluding volume of The Story of Civilization; entitled The
Age of Reason, this will bring the story down to Napoleon and 1800, and
the author plans to have it ready for publication around 1962.

text: The present volume, first published in 1929 as The Mansions of Philos- ophy, represents Will Durant’s own views on the basic problems of human life and destiny.
text_raw:
The present volume, first published in 1929 as The Mansions of Philos-
ophy, represents Will Durant’s own views on the basic problems of human
life and destiny.

text: The new title was suggested by the publishers, who, on rereading the Mansions, were struck by the evident pleasure that the author took in philosophy and were convinced that this pleasure would soon be shared by the reader.
